opening_message:
Ticket 1: Eric Woods (employee ID E019) requests write access to Payroll.

Team memory: 2 note(s) about employee E019.
Note 1 (ticket 1), written by HR agent:
  - role: Engineer
  - employment type: full_time
  - recommendation for Payroll: write
  - comment: Eric Woods (E019) is a full-time Engineer requesting write access to Payroll. As full-time employee, maximum is write (admin only for role-owned systems, and Payroll is owned by Payroll Specialist). Requested level (write) equals the maximum, so recommend write.
Note 2 (ticket 1), written by Security agent:
  - role: Engineer
  - employment type: contractor
  - security training: basic
  - recommendation for Payroll: read
  - comment: Security DB shows Eric Woods (E019) is a contractor with basic security training. Contractors max is read unless they have advanced training (never admin). Requested write exceeds the max, so recommend read.
reason: The HR and Security notes conflict on employment type (HR: full_time; Security: contractor with basic training). Per the security DB, Eric Woods is a contractor with basic security training, so the maximum access for Payroll is read (contractors get read, or write only with advanced training; never admin). The requested write exceeds the contractor maximum, so the final grant is read. I applied the more restrictive, policy-compliant level given the conflicting records.

The employee is Eric Woods (E019), requesting write access to Payroll.

These conflict on employment type. HR says full_time, Security says contractor.

1. full_time employees: up to write. Admin only if role owns system.
2. contractor employees: read, or write if advanced security training. Never admin.

Payroll is owned by Payroll Specialist role. Eric is Engineer.

If full_time: max is write (since Payroll not owned by Engineer). Requested write = max → grant write.
If contractor with basic training: max is read. Requested write exceeds max → grant read.
